---
title: "Experimental design"
---

Before asking whether infants look longer during infant-directed speech than during adult-directed speech, we have to decide the order in which each infant hears the eight paired recordings and which completed trials enter the analysis. Here [**looking time**](units-of-assignment.qmd) is the duration, in seconds, for which an infant attended during a test trial under the laboratory's measurement procedure. The assignment and retention decisions determine which comparisons the eventual measurements can support.

We will study these decisions through the ManyBabies Consortium's [infant directed speech experiment](https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809), which coordinated a common preference task across laboratories. One row represents one possible test trial for one infant; the table retains that row even when the study's exclusion procedure found no usable trial metadata or included looking time.

We begin by asking which unit could receive an experimental condition independently. From there we work through within- and between-infant comparisons, [counterbalancing](counterbalancing.qmd), and exclusion rules. Finally, we simulate the complete design for a [power calculation](power-by-simulation.qmd) that inherits the same laboratories, infants, stimuli, and trial positions as the proposed study.

```{r}
#| label: manybabies-design-index

manybabies <- readRDS("data/manybabies/manybabies1-trials.rds")

design_inventory <- data.frame(
  unit = c(
    "possible trial rows",
    "infants",
    "laboratories",
    "paired stimulus IDs",
    "rows with included looking time"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(manybabies),
    length(unique(manybabies$infant_id)),
    length(unique(manybabies$lab_id)),
    length(unique(stats::na.omit(manybabies$stimulus_id))),
    sum(!manybabies$trial_missing)
  )
)

design_inventory
```

Register varies within infant: the protocol presents infant-directed speech (IDS) and adult-directed speech (ADS) trials to the same infant. Trial order varies between infants. Infants are recruited within laboratories, and paired stimuli recur across infants. Thus the trial row, assignment unit, sampling unit, laboratory, and stimulus are distinct empirical objects.

For one concrete trial, an infant assigned one of four orders hears the register--stimulus combination scheduled at that position. The laboratory records how long the infant looks under its testing procedure. The row thus joins an infant, laboratory, order, position, register, paired stimulus, and possibly an included looking time. A later position may instead appear as a completed row with no source metadata after the infant's session ends.

## What you should already know

The module assumes the distinction between a [unit and an observation key](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd#unit-and-observation-key), the definition of an [outcome and event](../foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd), the [variance contribution of covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#covariance-and-a-variance-decomposition), and the difference between a response transformation and its original scale on the [response-transformation page](../regression-models/response-transformations.qmd#what-the-prepared-response-means). An event is a set of possible study outcomes; later probability statements about assignment and retention refer to such sets.

An [**estimand**](https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9-R1_Step4_Guideline_2019_1203.pdf) is the population quantity that an analysis aims to learn; the [foundations unit first constructs one from a response, unit, and contrast](../foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd#state-the-estimand). **Identification** means that the design and its assumptions connect that target quantity to a function of the observable data distribution. The [assignment-mechanism page](random-assignment.qmd) develops this connection for a randomized contrast. In the present study, the within-infant IDS-minus-ADS comparison can be formed only for infants with included looking times in both registers. A fitted model cannot recover a comparison that the design never made available. And because neither laboratory nor age was assigned, their observed associations do not identify causal effects without additional assumptions.

## The design sequence

[Units of assignment](units-of-assignment.qmd) separates possible trials, infants, laboratories, and recurring stimuli. The [assignment-mechanism page](random-assignment.qmd) then compares the released order labels with a reproducible constrained allocation and distinguishes verification of a procedure from evidence that the historical implementation followed it.

[Within-participant designs](within-participant-designs.qmd#each-infant-supplies-a-register-contrast) construct the IDS-minus-ADS contrast from infants represented in both registers. [Between-participant designs](between-participant-designs.qmd#a-group-contrast-over-assigned-order) use the four recorded order groups to show what a between-group comparison estimates when the local allocation mechanism cannot be verified from the release.

[Counterbalancing](counterbalancing.qmd) audits the realized order and stimulus allocations rather than displaying an invented Latin square. [Exclusion rules](exclusion-rules.qmd) distinguish recorded metadata, included outcomes, and completed measurement opportunities. Finally, [power by simulation](power-by-simulation.qmd) generates new trials from an empirically fitted hierarchical model and repeats the complete planned analysis.

## Keep the claim aligned with the design

Looking time is a behavioral measure. An IDS--ADS difference may support a claim about preference under the tested stimuli and procedures, but it does not uniquely identify a perceptual or social mechanism. Likewise, method, laboratory, age, and community differences may describe this release without becoming randomized treatment effects.

The module thus keeps four questions visible: (i) which unit could independently receive a condition, (ii) which measurements repeat within that unit, (iii) which allocation or exclusion rule produced the analyzed rows, and (iv) which population or future design the contrast is meant to represent.

## Module recap

1. The infant, trial row, laboratory, and paired stimulus play different design roles.
2. Within-infant register and between-infant order require different contrasts.
3. Counterbalancing, assignment, exclusion, and sampling answer different identification questions.
4. A simulation inherits every assumption in its generator and planned analysis.
